turns.player: Walk quietly and let the road speak — use Tremor Sense to read what moves on the hillside tonight
turns.summary: Adelheid walked the moonlit sluice-road, Tremor Sense confirming the Precursor pulse runs steadily beneath this ground too — south-southeast, unwavering, persistent.
turns.narration:
The sluice-road climbs in good stone — old-cut steps worn smooth in the middle, wild thyme pressing into the cracks. Moonlight comes down clean. Vreni walks a half-step ahead, her habit pale as birch bark, her sandals nearly silent.

You let your weight settle into each step and open the craft low, the way you'd lean an ear to a wall to hear the room beyond it. Tremor Sense reaches out into the hillside — not a push, just a receiving. What comes back: the slow, regular press of two deer moving through the coppice a hundred paces widdershins, the faint churn of water in the irrigation channel that runs alongside the road, the tiny percussion of mice in the terrace wall. The hill is ordinary and alive and unthreatened.

One thing is not ordinary. Running beneath the road, south-southeast the way the roots run, is the deep pulse — slower than a heartbeat, more patient than stone — the same Precursor vibration that hummed beneath the terrace. It is quieter here, farther from its surface expressions, but it is continuous and steady and absolutely present. It does not quicken when you listen. It simply persists, the way a river persists.

Aevi drifts close to your ear, her motes just bright enough to read. "Still same direction," she says, very quietly. "It runs under this road too." She dims back to near-nothing. Sister Vreni glances at the teal flicker but does not ask — a woman who has walked these hills long enough to know that some travelers carry things you do not inquire after, at night, on a steep road.

turns.player: Stop to listen more carefully where the road crosses a runnel — press both hands to the stone and read the pulse beneath it with Echo Sense
turns.summary: On the sluice-road above Millbrook, Adelheid pressed her hands to the stone at a drainage runnel and confirmed with Echo Sense that the Precursor pulse runs directly beneath the road — Aevi began unconsciously matching its rhythm.
turns.narration:
A thin runnel cuts across the road where the upper terrace drains — just wide enough to step over, the stone around it darker and cold. You pause there, crouch, and press both palms flat to the step.

Echo Sense opens outward through the rock — not through air, through stone — and what comes back is layered. The runnel itself, tracing a shallow path under the step and out through a weep-hole in the terrace wall. The deeper water of the irrigation channel, heavier and slower, running alongside the road a pace to your left. And beneath all of it, beneath the foundation cuts and the packed earth and the old mortar, the pulse. The same one you touched in the terrace two days ago. It runs here too, south-southeast, steady as a heartbeat that has never once faltered. Stronger than you expected — not because it has grown, but because the road sits directly over its line. The stone carries it faithfully.

Aevi drifts down from your shoulder and hovers just above the runnel, her motes dimming until they are almost gone — then brightening in a slow, regular rhythm. Once. Pause. Once. Pause. She is matching the pulse. She does not do it deliberately, you think; she does it the way a person hums to something they half-remember.

Vreni has stopped two steps ahead. She is looking back at you, unhurried, her hands folded into her sleeves. She does not ask what you are doing. She simply waits, with the particular patience of someone who has learned to let a healer work.

turns.player: Rise and walk on — save the questions for the wayhouse, where there's light and a hearth to sit beside
turns.summary: Adelheid rose from the runnel and walked on up the sluice-road with Vreni, the pulse left behind in the stone below — the wayhouse light waiting ahead.
turns.narration:
You lift your palms from the cold stone, dry them on your coat, and stand. The pulse is still there beneath your feet — you don't need both hands pressed flat to know it. It will be there tomorrow, and the day after, running its quiet south-southeast line toward the river. The wayhouse is an hour up the road, and there is a hearth there.

Vreni hears you rise. She doesn't turn immediately — just shifts her weight, a small adjustment that says she was paying attention without performing it. Then she starts walking again, sandals soft on the worn steps, and you fall in beside her. Aevi drifts upward from the runnel, her motes settling into their usual loose scatter at your shoulder. They are steady now, not dimming and brightening in that slow borrowed rhythm. Whatever the pulse was doing to her, the road breaks it.

The thyme smell comes and goes as you climb — stronger where the steps have been cracked and the roots have gotten in underneath. Above you the hillside opens a little, the coppice thinning, and the moonlight comes down brighter on the cut stone. Somewhere in the dark a nightjar calls once and is answered by nothing.

"The wayhouse keeps a light in the window," Vreni says, not loudly, just conversational in the night quiet. "You'll see it before you see the roof." She doesn't ask what you found at the runnel. She doesn't need to yet — there will be tea, and the kind of unhurried moment that a hearthside makes for speaking. The road climbs on, and the village lights are below you now, small and warm and far.

turns.player: Walk in companionable quiet and let the road finish itself — save all questions for the hearth
turns.summary: Adelheid and Sister Vreni reach the wayhouse at the top of the sluice-road — a low stone room with a working hearth, dried herbs in the rafters, and tea going on.
turns.narration:
The road gives you the rest of the hour without asking anything of you. Vreni sets the pace — unhurried, steady, the kind of walk that belongs to someone who has made this climb many times and long ago stopped counting them. The coppice thins above the terrace line and the sky opens wide: early-autumn stars, close and particular, the kind you only see when the valley below has put its lights to bed. Aevi drifts beside you, motes loose and quiet, casting just enough teal to pick out the thyme between the steps.

The wayhouse comes into view before you expect it — a low stone building set into the hillside on the far side of a flat shelf of cleared ground, one window lit amber from within. A thin thread of smoke from the chimney, rising straight in the still air. Vreni pushes the door open without ceremony and steps aside to let you through first, the way a host does when the house is already hers.

Inside: a single long room, stone flags, a trestle table with a candle at each end, a hearth with a proper fire going low and red. The smell of woodsmoke and dried herb — something in the rafters, something you'd have to stand on the table to name. Two pallets along the far wall, curtained off with undyed linen. A shelf of stoppered jars above the hearth, each labeled in a cramped hand. A good room. A working room.

Vreni fills a small iron pot from a covered ewer and sets it on the hearthstone without asking. "The tea is valerian and hops," she says, hanging her cloak on a peg by the door. "Enough to take the edge off a road. There's a second cup if you'd like it." She says it the way practical people say things — not as an offer requiring ceremony, just as information about what is available. Aevi settles on the shelf near the jar-row, motes dimming to a comfortable ember-glow, and the room is quiet and warm.

turns.player: Take the cup and look more carefully at the shelf of jars — read what medicines the wayhouse keeps and what it is short of
turns.summary: Adelheid takes her tea and reads the wayhouse medicine shelf — notes the gaps: no calendula, no lemon balm, no honey, and feverfew nearly spent.
turns.narration:
Vreni lifts the iron pot from the hearthstone and pours without ceremony — the valerian smell rises warm and a little bitter, and you take the cup in both hands. The heat settles into your fingers.

The jar shelf runs the full width of the wall above the hearth, each vessel stoppered with cork or wax and labeled in a cramped backward-slanting hand. You read along it while the tea cools: valerian-and-hops, already open and recently used; dried elderflower, a half-jar; plantain leaf, nearly full; yarrow, good stock; comfrey root, two jars — one almost gone, one sealed; a small dark bottle labeled simply *oil, clove*; feverfew, a pinch left at most; willow bark, a solid amount; and at the far end, a jar of what you recognize as dried meadowsweet by the pale florets still visible through the glass, a quarter-jar remaining. There is no calendula. No goldenrod. No lemon balm. No honey — none at all — and the small jar that might once have held it has been washed and left empty at the shelf's end, stopper out.

You know a wayhouse medicine shelf by what it runs short of. Feverfew nearly gone tells you headaches have been frequent — travelers coming in over the pass with altitude and tension both. The comfrey already cracked open says someone has been dealing with bruises or sprains. The missing honey is the quieter note: honey is a healer's glue and a sweetener both, and a house without it manages, but it feels the absence. Aevi drifts to the shelf's far end, her motes brightening faintly at the meadowsweet jar — curiosity, or just the warmth of the hearth.

Vreni watches you read the shelf the way you would watch someone speak a language you recognize. She does not interrupt.

turns.player: Tell Vreni plainly what the shelf is short of — name the gaps, offer what the Medic's Satchel can spare
turns.summary: Adelheid named the wayhouse's supply gaps and opened her satchel — Vreni accepted the offering and named the patient who is not quite as fine as he claims.
turns.narration:
You name them one by one, the way a working healer does — not a complaint, just a fact. Calendula, gone. Lemon balm, not there at all. Honey, the empty jar at the end. Feverfew down to a pinch, which is not enough for a fever that wants fighting. Goldenrod, absent.

Vreni listens without moving. Her eyes track the shelf as you speak, confirming each gap against her own knowledge of it — you can see her doing it, the small nods, the way her mouth tightens once at the feverfew. When you finish she is quiet for a moment, and then she says: "The comfrey has been doing the work of three things it was never meant to do." It is not an apology. It is the plain accounting of a house run hard.

You set down your cup and open the Medic's Satchel on the trestle table. What you have is modest but honest: a roll of dried yarrow flowers that will stretch the shelf's own stock, a folded paper of meadowsweet, a small stoppered vial of calendula-infused oil — not the dried flower, but something — and a square of pressed goldenrod wrapped in oilcloth. You lay them out side by side. "Not a resupply," you say, "but the gaps that matter most."

Vreni comes to the table. She picks up the calendula vial and holds it to the candle, reading the clarity of the oil. Then she sets it down carefully, exactly where it was, and looks at you. "The patient in the far pallet," she says, her voice dropping a register. "He came in two days ago with a wound on his forearm he says a farm tool made. I cleaned it and it closed well. But his pulse this morning was not what it was last night." She pauses. "He says he is fine. He is very insistent about it."

*You feel it settle into you — a new steadiness. (Level 2: +1 attunement, +5 reserves, and growth to choose — a sub-attribute point and a skill point.)*

turns.player: Sleep first — it is deep night, and a rested healer reads more than a tired one; ask Vreni to note his pulse at dawn and tell you the number
turns.summary: Adelheid slept the night at the wayhouse; Vreni will note the patient's dawn pulse.
turns.narration:
You tell Vreni plainly: wake me at first light with his pulse count, and you'll take the second set yourself after breakfast. She nods once — the nod of someone who already thought of it and is relieved to have been asked rather than having to suggest it herself. She shows you to the nearer curtained pallet, sets a second cup of tea on the small ledge beside it in case you wake in the night, and then moves back to the hearth without further ceremony.

Aevi drifts to the windowsill and dims almost entirely — the few motes that remain pulse very slowly, like a breath held and released. The dried herbs in the rafters smell of summer that has already passed: chamomile and something resinous you don't have a name for yet.

You are asleep before the candle on the trestle table burns to its collar.

quests.title: The Wyrm of Endings
quests.premise: The Ashen Wyrm has been seen on the far ridges — a dragon of the death-pole, hill-sized, its breath the grey stillness of everything stopping at once. Where it flies, the season ends. It does not hunt; it PASSES, and what it passes over is done. Keeper Ilma convenes the traditions: this dragon is the Ashwardens' own mercy become a weather, and it is a saga, not an encounter. The Wyrm is not an aberration but a symptom: the death-pole itself is leaning harder into its extreme, and the Ashen Wyrm is that pull made flesh — the edge of the world getting sharper, and hungrier for stillness.
quests.stakes: Domain-scale. A valley's worth of endings on the wing. The largest mercy the valley will ever be asked to give.

quests.title: The Patient Who Is Not Sick Enough
quests.premise: A man came down off the Mountain Pass road eleven days ago with a wound in his thigh that had been cleaned properly by somebody who knew how. It closed. He eats, he walks the court, he thanks people. Sister Vreni cannot say what is wrong and will not say he is well, and she has stopped being able to sleep about it. She is asking you because she has read your hands and because the house has nobody else who was trained to look at a person rather than at a wound.
quests.stakes: He has perhaps four days of looking fine left. What treats him grows on the high terraces the house has not harvested in two seasons, beside something that looks very like it and will finish him faster than the thing in his blood. And he is not called what he says he is, which is the second reason two parties have come to the gate asking after him politely.

stages.title: He looks well, and he is not
stages.objective: Assess him properly rather than looking at the wound. Count a resting pulse and count it again; watch the colour come back into a pressed nailbed; put the back of your hand on him. The wound is clean and closed and is not the problem, and the numbers are the only thing in the room that is telling the truth.
stages.condition: Take a full set of observations on Danic twice, at least six hours apart — or have Sister Vreni take the second set while you sleep.
stages.change: Codex: his pulse is fast and getting faster, his skin is warm and dry and then cool and damp, and the colour is slower back into the nailbed than it was this morning. His blood pressure has not moved, and that is the frightening part: a body this good at compensating is a body spending everything it has to look ordinary.

personalArc.name: The Root Remembers
personalArc.premise: A Swiss herbalist transplanted to an alien soil carries a silver-stemmed cutting from her village — the last living thread to everything she understood — and must decide whether her knowledge is a heritage to preserve or a seed to break open and replant entirely, in ground that does not know her name.
personalArc.stakes: To remain the keeper of a dead village's remedies, or to become something that village never imagined: a healer fluent in two earths, whose hands hold the old world and the new one at once — or to lose both trying.

stages.objective: the cutting that will not root — she has tried three times; the Korean soil rejects it, or she does not yet know how to ask; Mara Wells has seen this particular grief before, in other hands, and says so plainly

the remedy that should not work — she compounds a draught from Korean plants she only half-understands, borrowing Piotr's hard-won field notes, and it heals something her Swiss formulary swore was untreatable; the success feels like a betrayal, and a door

the linen unwrapped — the cutting is failing; she must choose what she owes it, what she owes Millbrook, and what she owes the healer she is becoming; the answer is in what she does with the roots when she finally opens the wrapping and faces what is left

picks.why: This is the aspiration they declared at 6/10 progress — they said they wanted it, it's reachable now, and it gives their sound-craft a restorative dimension their all-sensing, no-healing kit entirely lacks.

A cerebral, strategic mason who leans hard on Echo Sense and Tremor Sense already reads spaces through vibration — Sound Read adds structural diagnosis by touch, deepening exactly the information-gathering mode they actually play in, for just 1pt.

They have no way to appraise or protect against deception about materials and objects — a strategist-scholar who never uses Stillness Field or Drumline Stride is clearly not a mover or blocker, but a reader; Thingcraft fills the material-truth gap their sonic senses can't cover when a thing is still.

At 1pt it costs half what most picks do, flows directly from their mason domain in the same plain-method school they already train, and adds tactile material-truth to complement the acoustic truth they already hold — a natural, low-cost deepening of their signature information stack.

_suggestCache.note: They have 2 skill points and Chord of Mending is the declared destination — taking it now is the move; the remaining 0pt (or 1pt if Stone-Read pairs with it) leaves little room to add more this level, so the real choice is: claim the aspiration now, or bank toward a richer combo next level.
